title: Thrashing & Working Set
summary: Why over-multiprogramming can make a system spend nearly all its time paging instead of computing, and the two classic strategies — working set and page-fault frequency — that catch it before it happens.

slides.markdown:
Every page replacement algorithm from the last topic assumes the system is merely under *some* memory pressure — enough to require eviction decisions, but not so much that eviction itself becomes the bottleneck. **Thrashing** is what happens when that assumption breaks: the total memory processes actively need exceeds what's physically available, so the system spends more time paging pages in and out than running any actual instructions.

The fix isn't a smarter replacement algorithm — no policy can conjure memory that doesn't exist. It's admission control: know how much memory each process genuinely needs *right now* (the **working set**) and don't run more processes than fit, which is a fundamentally different kind of decision than "which page to evict."

slides.sectionTitle: Thrashing: spending more time paging than computing
slides.markdown:
**Thrashing** occurs when a process (or the whole system) doesn't have enough resident frames to hold its actively-used pages, so it faults constantly — every fault means evicting some other needed page, which itself gets faulted back in shortly after, evicting yet another needed page, in a self-reinforcing cycle.

The defining symptom is a system that looks *busy* (high paging I/O, the disk light constantly on) while getting almost nothing done — CPU utilization can actually **drop** even though load hasn't decreased, because processes spend nearly all their time blocked waiting on page faults rather than running. This is the scenario the effective-access-time math from Demand Paging describes at its worst: fault rate so high that it dominates everything.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: CPU utilization vs degree of multiprogramming, the thrashing cliff
slides.markdown:
![CPU utilization collapsing past the thrashing point](assets/thrashing-cliff-curve.svg)

The cliff shape is the whole point: utilization doesn't degrade gracefully past the peak, it collapses — which is exactly why thrashing feels sudden in production rather than a gradual slowdown.

slides.sectionTitle: Why increasing multiprogramming can cause thrashing, not fix it
slides.markdown:
A classic, dangerously plausible reaction to low CPU utilization is to add *more* processes, on the theory that more work in flight should keep the CPU busier. Below the thrashing cliff, that's correct — more processes genuinely improve utilization by giving the scheduler more to run whenever one process blocks.

Past the cliff, it backfires completely: each new process needs its own share of frames, so adding one takes frames away from processes that already had barely enough, pushing *them* into faulting more. Those extra faults mean more time blocked on I/O, which a naive utilization-based scheduler reads as "the CPU is idle, add more work" — accelerating the exact collapse it was trying to fix. This is the mechanism behind the falling half of the previous slide's cliff.

slides.sectionTitle: The working set model: the pages a process actually needs "now"
slides.markdown:
The **working set** of a process at a given time is the set of pages it has referenced in the most recent window of its execution — an empirical stand-in for "the pages this process needs resident right now to run without constantly faulting," based on the same locality principle LRU relies on.

The working set model's core policy: never run a process unless there are enough free frames to hold its *entire current working set*. If a process's working set doesn't fit, don't schedule it at all — this trades a smaller degree of multiprogramming for keeping every currently-running process comfortably resident, which is the direct fix for the over-multiprogramming that causes thrashing in the first place.

slides.sectionTitle: Working set size and the window parameter
slides.markdown:
The working set is defined relative to a **window** — Δ (delta) references (or a time interval) looking backward from now. A small Δ tracks very recent behavior closely but can undercount a process's real needs if it happens to be mid-loop with a small recent footprint; a large Δ smooths out noise but can overcount by including pages the process genuinely doesn't need anymore.

Choosing Δ is a real tuning trade-off with no universally correct value — too small and the model constantly evicts pages a process is about to reference again soon (thrashing at the model level, ironically); too large and it wastes memory holding pages that aren't actually needed, hurting the very multiprogramming degree the model exists to protect.

slides.sectionTitle: Page-Fault Frequency (PFF) as an alternative control strategy
slides.markdown:
**Page-Fault Frequency (PFF)** takes a more direct approach than modeling working sets explicitly: monitor each process's actual fault rate, and react to it. If a process's fault rate climbs above an upper threshold, it needs more frames — give it some (taken from a process well below the threshold, or by reducing the degree of multiprogramming if none are available). If a process's fault rate drops below a lower threshold, it has more frames than it needs — take some away.

This sidesteps having to define or measure a working set explicitly; the fault rate itself is treated as the signal, on the theory that a process with too few frames will show it directly through faulting. The trade-off is reactivity: PFF responds *after* faulting has already started climbing, whereas working set tries to prevent the situation by refusing to schedule an under-resourced process in the first place.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: working set vs PFF approaches to controlling thrashing
slides.markdown:
| | Working Set Model | Page-Fault Frequency (PFF) |
|---|---|---|
| Core signal | Which pages were referenced in the last Δ window | The process's observed fault rate |
| When it acts | Before scheduling — refuses to run an under-resourced process | After faulting starts — reacts to a rate crossing a threshold |
| Needs an explicit model of "which pages" | Yes, tracked per process | No — treats fault rate as a proxy, doesn't track specific pages |
| Tuning parameter | Window size Δ | Upper/lower fault-rate thresholds |
| Weakness | Expensive to track exact reference windows precisely | Reactive — some thrashing may already have happened before it responds |

Both are answering the same underlying question — how many frames does this process actually need — from different directions: working set estimates it proactively from access history, PFF infers it reactively from fault behavior.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: adding more processes to a thrashing system to "use the CPU better"
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "CPU utilization is low, so the system must have spare capacity — let's schedule more work to use it."

**Why it's wrong:** low CPU utilization has two completely different causes that look identical from a one-number dashboard — genuinely spare capacity (below the thrashing cliff, more work helps) or thrashing (past the cliff, the CPU is idle because processes are blocked on page faults, and more work makes it dramatically worse). Reacting the same way to both is exactly backward for the second case.

**Correct model:** check the paging/fault rate alongside CPU utilization before concluding there's spare capacity. Rising fault rate plus falling CPU utilization is the thrashing signature specifically — the fix there is running *fewer* processes (or giving existing ones more memory), the opposite of the naive reaction.

slides.sectionTitle: How this shows up in production: container memory limits and cgroup thrashing
slides.markdown:
Thrashing isn't just a textbook OS-course scenario — it's a real, recurring production failure mode in containerized environments. A container given a memory limit tighter than its actual working set will thrash against that limit: the kernel's cgroup memory controller reclaims pages aggressively once the limit is approached, and if the workload's genuine active footprint exceeds the limit, it faults or gets reclaimed from continuously, showing up as a service with high CPU-throttling-looking symptoms that's actually memory-bound, not CPU-bound.

The practical diagnostic habit worth having: a container or pod showing degraded throughput with paging/reclaim metrics climbing (not CPU throttling metrics) is a thrashing symptom, and the fix is raising the memory limit or reducing the workload's footprint — not adding CPU, which won't help a process that's blocked on page faults rather than compute-bound.
